Suppose \(0<\eta\le 1/4\). In \(\mathfrak E_3\), the two arrays \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\) are nonnegative, have \((D(0),R(1))\) margins \(f^-\) and \(f^+\), have \((D(1),R(1))\) margin \(\mu_1^\star\), and put mass only on \(D(0)\le D(1)\); with \(R(0)=\infty\), each is therefore a feasible full-law lift preserving both displayed within-arm tables. The displayed row sums, column sums, and complete chain-load matrices certify every marked-capacity constraint. The exact coordinate intervals are \(	heta_
u(1,1)\in[1/15,4/15]\), \(	heta_
u(2,2)\in[1/10,1/2]\), and \(	heta_
u(3,3)\in[1/5,4/5]\). For an arbitrary feasible \(f_{ij}\), \(\ell_\star(
u)=f_{10}-f_{21}+f_{30}+f_{32}\), \(\ell_\star(
u)\le f_{10}+f_{30}+f_{32}\le\kappa^\star_{00}+\kappa^\star_{22}=1/4\), while \(f_{21}+f_{31}\le1/10\) and \(f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32}=1/4-f_{33}\ge1/20\) imply \(\ell_\star(
u)\ge-1/20\). The arrays \(q^-_{ihj}\) and \(q^+_{ihj}\) attain these two endpoints, so the sharp interval is \([-1/20,1/4]\), strictly inside the coordinate rectangle \([-3/20,7/20]\). Replacing each finite atom by a sufficiently narrow separated symmetric bump and using a common bump draw when the two death categories agree yields a bounded-Lipschitz law satisfying all maintained conditions with the same strict separation; the separation persists on a relatively open neighborhood.
body.justification: A robust strict example establishes that the joint surface theorem adds identifying content beyond a collection of exact pointwise intervals.
body.gap: Generic warnings that pointwise sharp bounds need not be jointly sharp do not give a legal semicompeting-risk region with binding survivor capacities and exact support certificates.
body.consumer: It tells applied users when horizon-by-horizon uncertainty bands are mathematically incompatible and can reverse conclusions about signed clinical summaries.
body.proof_tex:
We give an exact finite-table certificate and then a smoothing construction.  All probabilities in the finite calculation are conditional on the sole value of \(X\), so the covariate subscript can be suppressed.

First consider the primitive exhibit \(\mathfrak E_3\).  Because \(R(0)=\infty\), the control numerator in the definition of the TV-SACE surface is
\[
b(r,t)=\Pr\{R(0)\le r,D(0)>t\}=0
\]
at every finite \(r\).  The four control death rows each have mass \(1/4\); hence
\[
S(1)=\frac34,\qquad S(2)=\frac12,\qquad S(3)=\frac14.
\]
Thus \(0<\eta\le 1/4\) puts \((1,1),(2,2),(3,3)\) in \(\mathcal H_\eta\), including the boundary case \(S(3)=\eta=1/4\).

Write \(f=(f_{ij})\) for an arbitrary feasible projected coupling and define the three unstandardized treated numerators
\[
A_1=\sum_{i>0}f_{i0},\qquad
A_2=\sum_{\substack{i>1\\j\le1}}f_{ij},\qquad
A_3=\sum_{j\le2}f_{3j}.
\]
The singleton marked-capacity inequalities in the grid characterization give
\[
A_1\le\kappa^\star_{00}=\frac15.
\]
Since the total demand in rows \(i>0\) is \(3/4\), while the other three marked tails across the first death cut have total capacity
\[
\kappa^\star_{01}+\kappa^\star_{02}+\kappa^\star_{03}
=\frac15+\frac3{20}+\frac7{20}=\frac7{10},
\]
the same inequalities also give
\[
A_1
=\frac34-\sum_{j=1}^3\sum_{i>0}f_{ij}
\ge\frac34-\frac7{10}=\frac1{20}.
\]
At the second death cut,
\[
A_2\le\kappa^\star_{10}+\kappa^\star_{11}
=\frac3{20}+\frac1{10}=\frac14.
\]
The total mass in rows \(i>1\) is \(1/2\), and the capacity available in columns \(2,3\) across that cut is \(3/20+3/10=9/20\).  Consequently
\[
A_2
=\frac12-\sum_{j=2}^3\sum_{i>1}f_{ij}
\ge\frac12-\frac9{20}=\frac1{20}.
\]
Finally, the third-cut capacities and the last-row demand imply
\[
A_3\le\kappa^\star_{20}+\kappa^\star_{21}+\kappa^\star_{22}
=\frac1{10}+\frac1{20}+\frac1{20}=\frac15
\]
and
\[
A_3=\frac14-f_{33}\ge\frac14-\kappa^\star_{23}
=\frac14-\frac15=\frac1{20}.
\]

These six inequalities are sharp.  The displayed flow \(f^+\) attains the upper endpoints for \(A_1\) and \(A_3\), whereas \(f^-\) attains the upper endpoint for \(A_2\) and the lower endpoint for \(A_3\).  For the two remaining lower endpoints, consider the arrays
\[
100g^{(1)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\
0&15&5&5\\
0&0&5&20\\
5&5&5&10
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
100g^{(2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\
0&20&0&5\\
0&0&10&15\\
5&0&5&15
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have row sums \((25,25,25,25)/100\) and column sums \((25,20,15,40)/100\).  Their complete singleton chain loads, again multiplied by \(100\), are
\[
\left(\sum_{i>k}g^{(1)}_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&20&15&35\\
5&5&10&30\\
5&5&5&10
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\left(\sum_{i>k}g^{(2)}_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&20&15&35\\
5&0&15&30\\
5&0&5&15
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each entry is no larger than the corresponding entry of \(100\kappa^\star\).  Hence both arrays are feasible by \(\mathrm{thm{:}quadratic\text{-}chain\text{-}flow}\); \(g^{(1)}\) has \(A_1=1/20\), and \(g^{(2)}\) has \(A_2=1/20\).  The feasible flow set is convex because its margins are affine equalities and its capacities and nonnegativity restrictions are linear inequalities.  The image of that set under each linear map \(f\mapsto A_j\) is therefore an interval, and the endpoint constructions prove
\[
A_1\in\left[\frac1{20},\frac15\right],\qquad
A_2\in\left[\frac1{20},\frac14\right],\qquad
A_3\in\left[\frac1{20},\frac15\right].
\]
Dividing by the strictly positive survivor masses displayed above, as required by the definition of \(\theta_\nu\), yields the exact coordinate intervals
\[
\theta_\nu(1,1)\in\left[\frac1{15},\frac4{15}\right],\qquad
\theta_\nu(2,2)\in\left[\frac1{10},\frac12\right],\qquad
\theta_\nu(3,3)\in\left[\frac15,\frac45\right].
\]

We next verify the two claimed full-law lifts.  Direct summation of the nonzero entries specified in the definition gives
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^-_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
10&0&10&5\\
0&10&5&10\\
15&5&0&5\\
0&5&0&20
\end{pmatrix}
=100f^-,
\]
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^+_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&0&10&10\\
10&15&0&0\\
0&0&0&25\\
10&5&5&5
\end{pmatrix}
=100f^+,
\]
and, for both signs,
\[
100\left(\sum_iq^\pm_{ihj}\right)_{hj}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&0&0&5\\
5&10&0&5\\
5&5&10&10\\
10&5&5&20
\end{pmatrix}
=100\mu_1^\star.
\]
Every listed entry is nonnegative.  The first two displays prove the asserted \((D(0),R(1))\) margins, and the third proves the treated \((D(1),R(1))\) margin.  Summing either \(f^\pm\) across its readmission columns gives the control death margin \((1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4)\).  After setting \(R(0)=\infty\), this is exactly \(\mu_0^\star\).  Inspection of every listed positive triple gives \(i\le h\), so its support satisfies \(D(0)\le D(1)\).  The positive cells of \(\mu_1^\star\) also have \(r_j^\star<d_h^\star\) whenever \(r_j^\star<\infty\), and the control order is vacuous because \(R(0)=\infty\).  Thus both lifts obey the semicompeting-risk order.

For completeness, the row sums and column sums of \(f^\pm\) are respectively
\[
\left(\frac14,\frac14,\frac14,\frac14\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left(\frac14,\frac15,\frac3{20},\frac25\right).
\]
Their singleton chain-load matrices are those displayed in the definition and are entrywise bounded by \(\kappa^\star\).  On this finite ordered support, every threshold \(u\) induces either one of the three nontrivial death cuts or a trivial cut.  Every Borel readmission-mark set induces a subset of the four atoms, and summing the valid singleton-column inequalities proves the inequality for that subset.  Hence the displayed checks certify all event-set capacity restrictions, not merely prefix restrictions.

We now calculate the genuinely joint support.  Substitution of \(S(1)=3/4\), \(S(2)=1/2\), \(S(3)=1/4\) into the signed direction gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_\star(\nu)
&=\sum_{i>0}f_{i0}
  -\sum_{\substack{i>1\\j\le1}}f_{ij}
  +\sum_{j\le2}f_{3j}\\
&=f_{10}-f_{21}+f_{30}+f_{32}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the upper endpoint, nonnegativity and the first and third cut capacities imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_\star(\nu)
&\le f_{10}+f_{30}+f_{32}\\
&\le \sum_{i>0}f_{i0}+\sum_{i>2}f_{i2}\\
&\le\kappa^\star_{00}+\kappa^\star_{22}
=\frac15+\frac1{20}=\frac14.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the lower endpoint, the second-cut capacity in column \(1\) and the last-row margin give
\[
f_{21}+f_{31}\le\kappa^\star_{11}=\frac1{10},
\qquad
f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32}
=\frac14-f_{33}
\ge\frac14-\kappa^\star_{23}=\frac1{20}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_\star(\nu)
&=f_{10}-(f_{21}+f_{31})+(f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32})\\
&\ge 0-\frac1{10}+\frac1{20}=-\frac1{20}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct substitution in the displayed flows gives
\[
\ell_\star(f^-)=-\frac1{20},
\qquad
\ell_\star(f^+)=\frac14.
\]
The full lifts already verified show that both endpoints are attainable under terminal monotonicity.  Convex mixing of the two full laws preserves both within-arm margins and every maintained structural restriction, so every intermediate value is attainable.  Thus the sharp signed support is exactly
\[
\left[-\frac1{20},\frac14\right].
\]

If the three coordinates could instead be varied independently over their exact marginal intervals, the smallest and largest values in the same signed direction would be
\[
\frac34\frac1{15}-\frac12\frac12+\frac14\frac15
=-\frac3{20}
\]
and
\[
\frac34\frac4{15}-\frac12\frac1{10}+\frac14\frac45
=\frac7{20},
\]
respectively.  Hence the coordinate rectangle has support interval
\[
\left[-\frac3{20},\frac7{20}\right],
\]
which strictly contains the sharp joint interval, with a gap \(1/10\) at each endpoint.

It remains to show that the certificate is compatible with the regularity assumptions and is not an atomic knife-edge example.  Choose a nonnegative symmetric continuously differentiable density \(\varphi_\delta\), of integral one and support contained in \((-\delta,\delta)\), where \(0<\delta<1/8\).  Replace every finite category by the corresponding translate of this density and leave the atom at \(\infty\) unchanged.  Conditional on a positive categorical lift cell \((i,h,j)\), use independent translated bump draws for the two finite death coordinates when \(i<h\), use the same death draw when \(i=h\), and take the readmission bump draw independently.  If a coordinate has category \(\infty\), leave it equal to \(\infty\).

This construction preserves every categorical mass in both within-arm margins.  If \(i<h\), adjacent finite death centers are one unit apart, so \(\delta<1/8\) implies \(D(0)<D(1)\); if \(i=h\), the shared draw implies \(D(0)=D(1)\).  The smallest gap between a finite treated readmission center and a compatible treated death center is \(1/4\).  Therefore
\[
\sup R(1)\le r_j^\star+\delta
<d_h^\star-\delta\le\inf D(1)
\]
inside every cell with finite readmission, because \(2\delta<1/4\).  The semicompeting order is thus preserved.  Finite-part marginal densities are finite mixtures of translates of \(\varphi_\delta\), and finite-part joint densities are finite mixtures of products of such translates.  They consequently have finite sup-norm and Lipschitz constants; choosing \(M\) and \(L_{\mathrm{Lip}}\) no smaller than these finite constants verifies the two density conditions.

The supports of the death bumps do not cross the integer thresholds \(1,2,3\), and the supports of the readmission bumps do not cross the corresponding readmission thresholds.  Consequently every indicator entering \(A_1,A_2,A_3\), every survivor denominator, and every capacity inequality used above has exactly its categorical value.  Conversely, every admissible smoothed full law projects at these thresholds to a categorical flow satisfying the same necessary capacity inequalities.  For attainability, apply the full-law lift part of \(\mathrm{thm{:}quadratic\text{-}chain\text{-}flow}\) to each categorical endpoint flow and then apply the preceding shared-bump construction to that lift.  Thus the six coordinate endpoints and the two signed endpoints remain attainable, and all the exact support calculations above remain valid for the smoothed law.

The remaining maintained sampling conditions hold explicitly: \(X\) is degenerate with positive mass, \(Z\) is independent of all potential variables with \(e=1/2\), factual outcomes are assigned by consistency, and \(C=\tau=3\) gives
\[
G_{zx}(u)=1\ge\gamma\qquad(0\le u\le\tau).
\]
In particular, censoring support is verified through the full analysis horizon rather than only before the last event.

Finally, keep the separated bump kernels and their structural incidence pattern fixed and vary their finitely many mixture weights within the feasible parameter cone.  The relevant coordinate and signed support problems then have a fixed finite constraint matrix, with the mixture weights entering only the right-hand side.  After slack variables are added, there are finitely many possible bases.  On the relative region where any one basis is feasible and optimal, its basic solution and its objective are affine functions of the weights; where optimality regions meet, their objective values agree.  The endpoint maps are therefore continuous and piecewise affine on this finite polyhedral parameter cone.  At the displayed law both strict gaps equal \(1/10\), so continuity leaves both gaps positive throughout a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood of the smoothed law.  This proves the asserted robust strict cross-cohort separation within the maintained monotonicity-restricted model.
